raw_response:
I have farmed these lands for 50 years, and I know every mu of my 5.5 mu plot. At 73, with only my wife and me in the house, I must be honest about what two old bodies can do. Cotton is in my bones—I have planted it since I was a young man—but it is a greedy crop. It needs spraying every few days when the bollworm comes, and picking it by hand under the hot sun bends my back. Still, I keep it because the price is steady and the buyer is reliable. Stevia is my main crop now. The company sends a truck to the edge of the village, and the price is better than cotton. It is thirsty and needs water, but cutting and drying the leaves is easier on my hands than plucking cotton bolls.

This year I will divide my land so that stevia gets the larger share: 3 mu for stevia and 2.5 mu for cotton. I have a well, so water is not my worry, but carrying the pump hose tires me out, so I plan my irrigations carefully. I will till both fields with the rotary tiller, the same machine I have hired for twenty years. For fertilizer, I will buy two bags of compound fertilizer from the cooperative for each mu—about 100 jin per mu—and spread it as a base. Cotton needs more food to keep growing into autumn, so I will add a little extra urea when it flowers. Pests are the real enemy here. Cotton will need about fourteen sprays in total to keep the worms and weeds at bay. Stevia is cleaner, maybe six sprays will do. I buy hybrid cotton seeds because they fight the worms better, and I buy improved stevia seedlings from the seed shop in town. I expect my cotton to give 550 jin per mu and my stevia to give 600 jin per mu if the weather is kind. My wife and I will do the work ourselves. We have always managed.
